name.text: Definition of inactive clause

questiontext.text: A major clause ci is inactive for predicate p (under a fixed assignment of the minor clauses) when:

answer.text: Toggling only ci, with the minor clauses fixed, does not change the value of p

feedback.text: Correct — an inactive clause does not determine p; flipping it leaves p unchanged.

answer.text: Toggling only ci, with the minor clauses fixed, changes the value of p

feedback.text: That is an active (determining) clause, the opposite of inactive.
Inactivity is about ci not affecting p, not about ci's own value.

answer.text: ci does not appear syntactically in p

feedback.text: An inactive clause is still part of p; it just happens to be masked by the minor clauses.

generalfeedback.text: A clause is inactive (does not determine p) under a minor assignment when flipping it, with everything else fixed, leaves p's value unchanged. This is exactly the negation of "determines".

name.text: Equivalent inactivity condition

questiontext.text: With the minor clauses fixed, clause ci is inactive for p if and only if:

feedback.text: Correct — p takes the same value whether ci is true or false, so ci has no effect.
That is the determination (active) condition, not inactivity.
Inactivity is about ci not changing p, not about them being equal.
Inactivity does not require the minor clauses to match ci.

generalfeedback.text: ci is inactive exactly when pci=T = pci=F under the fixed minor assignment: the two possible ci values give the same p, so ci does not determine p.

name.text: When a is inactive in a AND b

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∧ b, clause a is inactive exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — with b false, p is false regardless of a, so a does not determine p.
With b true, p equals a, so a determines p — a is active, not inactive.
When b is true, a does determine p, so a is not always inactive.
a is inactive whenever b is false.

generalfeedback.text: For a conjunction a ∧ b, clause a determines p only when b is true. Hence a is inactive exactly when b is false, where p is pinned to false.

name.text: When a is inactive in a OR b

questiontext.text: For predicate p = a ∨ b, clause a is inactive exactly when:

feedback.text: Correct — with b true, p is true regardless of a, so a does not determine p.
With b false, p equals a, so a determines p — a is active, not inactive.
When b is false, a determines p, so a is not always inactive.
a is inactive whenever b is true.

generalfeedback.text: For a disjunction a ∨ b, clause a determines p only when b is false. Hence a is inactive exactly when b is true, where p is pinned to true.

name.text: Inactive means does not determine

questiontext.text: A clause is inactive for a predicate exactly when it does not determine that predicate.

feedback.text: Correct — "inactive" is defined as the negation of "determines".
Inactive and determining are complementary: a clause is inactive precisely when it fails to determine p.

generalfeedback.text: Active-clause criteria require a clause to determine p; inactive-clause criteria require it to be masked. "Inactive" simply means the clause does not determine the predicate under the given minor assignment.

name.text: Purpose of inactive-clause coverage

questiontext.text: The inactive-clause criteria (GICC/RICC) are designed to verify that:

answer.text: An inactive (masked) clause genuinely has no effect on the predicate's outcome

feedback.text: Correct — they check that masking behaves correctly.

answer.text: Each clause independently determines the predicate

feedback.text: That is the goal of the active-clause criteria (GACC/CACC/RACC).

answer.text: Every combination of clause values is exercised

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage.

answer.text: The predicate takes both truth values at least once

feedback.text: That is merely Predicate Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Inactive-clause coverage confirms that when a clause is supposed to be masked, it really has no effect on p — catching bugs where a "don't care" clause secretly changes the outcome.

name.text: GICC acronym

questiontext.text: What does GICC stand for?

feedback.text: Correct.
The "I" stands for Inactive, not Independent.
That is GACC, an active-clause criterion.
Not a standard criterion name.

generalfeedback.text: GICC = General Inactive Clause Coverage: the inactive-clause criterion whose minor-clause values may differ across the four test requirements.

name.text: RICC acronym

questiontext.text: What does RICC stand for?

feedback.text: Correct.
The "I" stands for Inactive, not Independent.
That is RACC, an active-clause criterion.
Not a standard criterion name.

generalfeedback.text: RICC = Restricted Inactive Clause Coverage: like GICC, but the minor-clause values must match across the paired ci=true / ci=false requirements at each fixed value of p.

name.text: Number of ICC requirements per clause

questiontext.text: For each major clause, Inactive Clause Coverage imposes how many test requirements?

feedback.text: Correct — the four combinations of ci ∈ {T,F} with p ∈ {T,F}, all with ci inactive.
2 would only cover ci=true and ci=false; ICC also splits on p's value.
ICC needs four requirements per clause, not one.
2^n is Combinatorial Coverage, not ICC.

generalfeedback.text: Because an inactive clause does not determine p, p can independently be true or false. ICC therefore requires four requirements per major clause: ci=T∧p=T, ci=T∧p=F, ci=F∧p=T, ci=F∧p=F.

name.text: What the four ICC requirements vary

questiontext.text: The four Inactive Clause Coverage requirements for a major clause enumerate the combinations of:

answer.text: The value of ci (true/false) and the value of p (true/false)

feedback.text: Correct — 2 × 2 = 4 requirements, all with ci inactive.

answer.text: The values of two of the minor clauses

feedback.text: ICC varies ci and p, not a pair of minor clauses.

answer.text: The value of ci and whether ci determines p

feedback.text: ci is inactive (does not determine p) in all four requirements; only ci and p vary.

answer.text: All 2^n rows of the truth table

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage.

generalfeedback.text: Holding ci inactive, ICC crosses ci ∈ {T,F} with p ∈ {T,F}, giving four requirements per major clause.

name.text: Value of a AND b when a is inactive

questiontext.text: For p = a ∧ b, when clause a is inactive (b = false), the predicate p is:

feedback.text: Correct — b false forces a ∧ b to false whatever a is.
A conjunction with a false operand is false, not true.
That happens when b is true (a active), not when a is inactive.
p is well-defined and equals false.

generalfeedback.text: Making a inactive in a ∧ b requires b = false, which pins p to false. So while a is inactive, p can only be false — a fact with consequences for ICC feasibility.

name.text: Value of a OR b when a is inactive

questiontext.text: For p = a ∨ b, when clause a is inactive (b = true), the predicate p is:

feedback.text: Correct — b true forces a ∨ b to true whatever a is.
A disjunction with a true operand is true, not false.
That happens when b is false (a active), not when a is inactive.
p is well-defined and equals true.

generalfeedback.text: Making a inactive in a ∨ b requires b = true, which pins p to true. So while a is inactive, p can only be true — the dual of the conjunction case.

name.text: Minor clauses determine p when masked

questiontext.text: When a major clause is inactive, the predicate's value is determined entirely by the minor clauses.

feedback.text: Correct — since the major clause has no effect, only the minor clauses fix p.
An inactive major clause cannot change p, so p is fixed by the minor clauses alone.

generalfeedback.text: An inactive clause does not affect p, so with it masked the outcome is a function of the minor clauses only. This is why, while ci is inactive, p can still independently be true or false depending on the minor clauses.

name.text: Contrast with active-clause coverage

questiontext.text: Which family of criteria is the direct contrast to the inactive-clause criteria?

feedback.text: Correct — they require the clause to determine p, whereas inactive-clause criteria require it to be masked.
Those are coarser criteria, not the active/inactive counterpart.
CoC exercises all combinations; it is not the determination-based counterpart.
Those are a separate DNF-based family, not the direct contrast.

generalfeedback.text: The active-clause criteria (GACC/CACC/RACC) require each clause to determine p; the inactive-clause criteria (GICC/RICC) require each clause to be masked. They are complementary halves of the determination idea.

name.text: b false makes a active in a OR b

questiontext.text: For p = a ∨ b, setting b = false makes clause a active (determining), not inactive.

feedback.text: Correct — with b false, p equals a, so a determines p.
With b false, p = a ∨ false = a, so flipping a flips p; a is active. a would be inactive when b = true.

generalfeedback.text: For a ∨ b, a is inactive when b = true (p pinned to true) and active when b = false (p mirrors a).

name.text: Make c inactive in (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, which minor assignment makes clause c inactive?

feedback.text: Correct — then a ∧ b is true, so p is true regardless of c; c is masked.
Then a ∧ b is false, so p = c and c determines p (active).
Then a ∧ b is false, so p = c and c is active.
Then a ∧ b is false, so p = c and c is active.

generalfeedback.text: For a disjunction X ∨ c, clause c is inactive exactly when the other operand X is true. Here X = a ∧ b, so c is inactive when a = true and b = true.

name.text: When a determines (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, which minor assignment makes clause a active (i.e., a is not inactive)?

feedback.text: Correct — only then does p reduce to a, so a determines p.
With b false, a ∧ b is false regardless of a, so a is inactive.
c true pins p to true and b false masks a, so a is inactive.
c true pins p to true regardless of a, so a is inactive.

generalfeedback.text: a determines p only when its term passes a through (b = true) and the disjunction does not mask it (c = false). At every other minor assignment, a is inactive.

name.text: The four ICC requirements

questiontext.text: For an inactive major clause ci, Inactive Clause Coverage requires test requirements covering exactly:

feedback.text: Correct — ci and p each take both values while ci stays inactive.
That ignores the requirement that p also take both values.
That ignores the requirement that ci also take both values.

answer.text: All 2^n combinations of the clause values

feedback.text: That is Combinatorial Coverage, not ICC.

generalfeedback.text: Because an inactive clause cannot change p, p is free to be true or false independently of ci. ICC therefore lists all four (ci, p) combinations as separate test requirements.

name.text: How RICC restricts GICC

questiontext.text: How does Restricted Inactive Clause Coverage (RICC) differ from General Inactive Clause Coverage (GICC)?

answer.text: RICC requires the minor-clause values to be identical for the ci=true and ci=false requirements that share the same value of p

feedback.text: Correct — RICC pins the minors across each same-p pair; GICC lets them vary.

answer.text: RICC requires the minor-clause values to differ across all four requirements

feedback.text: RICC constrains minors to be the same across the same-p pairs, not different.

answer.text: RICC requires ci to determine p

feedback.text: Both are inactive-clause criteria: ci is masked in both, never determining p.

answer.text: RICC drops one of the four requirements

feedback.text: RICC keeps all four requirements; it only adds a constraint on the minor clauses.

generalfeedback.text: GICC lets the minor-clause values vary freely among the four requirements. RICC adds the restriction that the minors match within each same-p pair (ci=T∧p=T with ci=F∧p=T, and ci=T∧p=F with ci=F∧p=F).

name.text: Active vs inactive requirement

questiontext.text: The active-clause criteria require the major clause to determine p. The inactive-clause criteria instead require the major clause to:

answer.text: Not determine p (be masked by the minor clauses)

feedback.text: Correct — inactive-clause coverage exercises the masked case.
That is the active-clause idea, the opposite of inactive.

answer.text: Take the same value as p

feedback.text: Masking is not about the clause equalling p.
The clause stays in the predicate; it is merely masked at runtime.

generalfeedback.text: Active-clause criteria set the minor clauses so ci determines p; inactive-clause criteria set them so ci is masked and cannot affect p.

name.text: Make a inactive in a OR (b AND c)

questiontext.text: For p = a ∨ (b ∧ c), which minor assignment makes clause a inactive?

feedback.text: Correct — then b ∧ c is true, so p is true regardless of a; a is masked.
Then b ∧ c is false, so p = a and a determines p (active).
Then b ∧ c is false, so p = a and a is active.
Then b ∧ c is false, so p = a and a is active.

generalfeedback.text: For a disjunction a ∨ X, clause a is inactive exactly when the other operand X is true. Here X = b ∧ c, so a is inactive when b = true and c = true.

name.text: Make c inactive in (a OR b) AND c

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∨ b) ∧ c, which minor assignment makes clause c inactive?

feedback.text: Correct — then a ∨ b is false, so p is false regardless of c; c is masked.
Then a ∨ b is true, so p = c and c determines p (active).
Then a ∨ b is true, so p = c and c is active.
Then a ∨ b is true, so p = c and c is active.

generalfeedback.text: For a conjunction X ∧ c, clause c is inactive exactly when the other operand X is false. Here X = a ∨ b, so c is inactive when a = false and b = false.

name.text: Tests for four feasible ICC requirements

questiontext.text: When all four Inactive Clause Coverage requirements for a single major clause are feasible, how many distinct test cases are needed to satisfy them?

feedback.text: Correct — the four (ci, p) combinations are distinct, so four tests are required.
Two tests cannot realise four different (ci, p) combinations.
Three tests leave one of the four (ci, p) combinations uncovered.
One test fixes a single (ci, p) pair, not all four.

generalfeedback.text: Each of the four requirements pins a distinct pair of (ci value, p value); no single test can satisfy two of them at once, so four tests are needed for that clause.

name.text: Which clause is inactive at a row

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c evaluated at a = true, b = false, c = false, which clause is inactive (does not determine p)?

feedback.text: Correct — flipping a gives (F ∧ F) ∨ F = F, unchanged from p = F, so a is inactive here.
Flipping b gives (T ∧ T) ∨ F = T, changing p from F, so b is active here.
Flipping c gives (T ∧ F) ∨ T = T, changing p from F, so c is active here.
a is inactive at this row; b and c are active.

generalfeedback.text: At a=T, b=F, c=F, p = (T∧F)∨F = F. Flipping a leaves p false (a masked by b=F), while flipping b or c changes p. So a is the only inactive clause here.

name.text: RICC pairing at p true

questiontext.text: Under RICC, the two requirements with ci=true and ci=false at p=true must:

answer.text: Use the same values for all minor clauses

feedback.text: Correct — RICC pins the minor clauses across each same-p pair.

answer.text: Use different values for the minor clauses

feedback.text: That is not required by any criterion; RICC pins them equal.
These are inactive-clause requirements: ci stays masked.
Both requirements in this pair fix p = true.

generalfeedback.text: RICC requires the minor-clause values to match within each same-p pair. For the p=true pair, the ci=true and ci=false tests use identical minor values (which is exactly why p stays true across the pair).

name.text: GICC minors may vary

questiontext.text: Under GICC, the minor-clause values may differ across the four inactive-clause test requirements.

feedback.text: Correct — GICC places no matching constraint on the minor clauses.
It is RICC, not GICC, that forces the minors to match; GICC lets them vary.

generalfeedback.text: GICC ("General") only requires that ci be inactive in each of the four requirements; the minor-clause values are free to change from one requirement to another.

name.text: Criterion that confirms masking

questiontext.text: Which criterion is specifically aimed at confirming the correct masking of a clause?

feedback.text: Correct — it checks that a masked clause has no effect on p.
CACC checks the clause's determining (active) effect, not masking.
GACC is an active-clause criterion; it exercises determination, not masking.
PC only requires p to take both values; it says nothing about masking.

generalfeedback.text: Only the inactive-clause criteria deliberately mask a clause and check that p is unaffected — the test for correct masking.

name.text: p value while a is inactive in a AND b

questiontext.text: For p = a ∧ b, across all minor assignments that make clause a inactive, the value of p is:

feedback.text: Correct — a is inactive only when b = false, and then p = false.
a is inactive when b = false, which forces p to false, not true.
There is only one masking assignment (b = false), and it pins p to false.
p equals a only when a is active (b = true).

generalfeedback.text: For a ∧ b the only way to mask a is b = false, which fixes p = false. Consequently the ICC requirements needing p = true for clause a are infeasible.

name.text: When a is not inactive in a OR b OR c

questiontext.text: For p = a ∨ b ∨ c, clause a fails to be inactive (it determines p) only when:

feedback.text: Correct — then p = a, so a determines p; at every other minor assignment a is masked.
Then p is true regardless of a, so a is inactive there.
b true pins p to true regardless of a, so a is inactive.
c true pins p to true regardless of a, so a is inactive.

generalfeedback.text: For a disjunction, a determines p only when every other operand is false. Here that means b = false and c = false; otherwise b ∨ c is true and a is masked.

name.text: Requirements a p-false masking helps

questiontext.text: Suppose a minor assignment makes ci inactive and pins p to false regardless of ci. Which ICC requirements can such an assignment help satisfy?

answer.text: The two requirements with p = false (ci=T∧p=F and ci=F∧p=F)

feedback.text: Correct — with p pinned false, only the p=false requirements can be met from this assignment.

answer.text: The two requirements with p = true

feedback.text: p is false here, so it cannot satisfy any p=true requirement.
Only the two p=false requirements are reachable when p is pinned false.
It does satisfy the p=false requirements (for both ci values).

generalfeedback.text: Because ci is inactive, both ci=T and ci=F are available at this assignment, but p is stuck at false — so it covers ci=T∧p=F and ci=F∧p=F only.

name.text: RICC subsumes GICC

questiontext.text: Restricted Inactive Clause Coverage (RICC) subsumes General Inactive Clause Coverage (GICC).

feedback.text: Correct — RICC's requirements are GICC's plus an extra minor-matching constraint, so any RICC-satisfying suite satisfies GICC.
RICC is strictly stronger: it adds a restriction to GICC, so RICC → GICC.

generalfeedback.text: RICC keeps all of GICC's four requirements and additionally forces the minor clauses to match within each same-p pair. A stricter criterion that only adds constraints subsumes the weaker one, so RICC subsumes GICC.

name.text: Why RICC subsumes GICC

questiontext.text: Why does RICC subsume GICC?

answer.text: RICC's test requirements are GICC's requirements plus an extra minor-matching constraint, so any suite meeting RICC also meets GICC

feedback.text: Correct — adding constraints can only shrink the set of satisfying suites.

answer.text: RICC has more test requirements than GICC

feedback.text: Both have the same four requirements per clause; RICC just constrains the minors more tightly.
That would be Combinatorial Coverage, not RICC.

answer.text: RICC additionally requires ci to determine p

feedback.text: Both are inactive-clause criteria; neither requires determination.

generalfeedback.text: Subsumption follows because RICC = GICC + (minors match within each same-p pair). Every RICC test set already satisfies the looser GICC obligations, so RICC subsumes GICC.

name.text: Inactive criteria subsume Clause Coverage

questiontext.text: Both GICC and RICC subsume Clause Coverage (CC).

feedback.text: Correct — each major clause is exercised both true and false (while inactive), which is exactly Clause Coverage.
GICC and RICC both require ci=true and ci=false requirements for every clause, so every clause takes both values — CC is met.

generalfeedback.text: The four ICC requirements include both ci=true and ci=false for each clause, so every clause takes both truth values. Hence GICC and RICC each subsume Clause Coverage.

name.text: Why GICC subsumes CC

questiontext.text: What makes GICC subsume Clause Coverage?

answer.text: For every clause, GICC requires a ci=true test and a ci=false test, so each clause takes both values

feedback.text: Correct — that is precisely the Clause Coverage requirement.

answer.text: GICC requires the predicate to take both values

feedback.text: That would relate to Predicate Coverage; CC is about individual clauses.
That is Combinatorial Coverage, stronger than needed for CC.

answer.text: GICC requires each clause to determine p

feedback.text: That is the active-clause idea; inactive-clause coverage masks the clause instead.

generalfeedback.text: Clause Coverage requires each clause to be both true and false. Because GICC's four requirements per clause include ci=true and ci=false, every clause is exercised both ways, so GICC subsumes CC.

name.text: Infeasible ICC requirements for a AND b

questiontext.text: For p = a ∧ b, which Inactive Clause Coverage requirements for clause a are infeasible?

answer.text: The two requiring p = true (a=T∧p=T and a=F∧p=T)

feedback.text: Correct — a can be inactive only when b = false, which pins p to false, so p = true is unreachable while a is inactive.
Those are the feasible ones: masking a (b = false) makes p = false.
The two p=false requirements are feasible; only the p=true ones are not.
a inactive forces p = false, so the p=true requirements cannot be met.

generalfeedback.text: Masking a in a ∧ b requires b = false, pinning p to false. Thus a=T∧p=T and a=F∧p=T are infeasible, while the two p=false requirements are feasible.

name.text: Infeasible ICC requirements for a OR b

questiontext.text: For p = a ∨ b, which Inactive Clause Coverage requirements for clause a are infeasible?

answer.text: The two requiring p = false (a=T∧p=F and a=F∧p=F)

feedback.text: Correct — a can be inactive only when b = true, which pins p to true, so p = false is unreachable while a is inactive.
Those are the feasible ones: masking a (b = true) makes p = true.
The two p=true requirements are feasible; only the p=false ones are not.
a inactive forces p = true, so the p=false requirements cannot be met.

generalfeedback.text: Masking a in a ∨ b requires b = true, pinning p to true. Thus a=T∧p=F and a=F∧p=F are infeasible, while the two p=true requirements are feasible.

name.text: Inactive rows for a in a AND b AND c

questiontext.text: For p = a ∧ b ∧ c, in how many of the 8 assignments is clause a inactive?

feedback.text: Correct — a determines p only when b ∧ c is true (2 rows), so a is inactive in the other 6.
2 is the number of rows where a is active (b=T, c=T), not inactive.
Recount — a is active only when b ∧ c is true, which is 2 rows, leaving 6 inactive.
a is active in 2 rows, so it is not inactive in all 8.

generalfeedback.text: a determines a ∧ b ∧ c exactly when b ∧ c is true (b=T, c=T), giving 2 active rows (a free). The remaining 6 of 8 rows have a inactive.

name.text: Inactive rows for c in (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, in how many of the 8 assignments is clause c inactive?

feedback.text: Correct — c is inactive only when a ∧ b is true (a=T, b=T), which is 2 rows (c free).
6 is the number of rows where c is active (a ∧ b false), not inactive.
Recount — a ∧ b is true in only 2 of the 8 rows.
Both c=T and c=F rows at a=T,b=T are inactive, giving 2, not 1.

generalfeedback.text: c is inactive exactly when the other operand a ∧ b is true. That happens in 2 of the 8 rows (a=T, b=T, c either value), so c is inactive in 2 assignments.

name.text: Inactive rows for a in (a AND b) OR (c AND d)

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d), in how many of the 16 assignments is clause a inactive?

feedback.text: Correct — a is active only when b = true and (c ∧ d) = false: 1 × 3 × 2 = 6 rows, leaving 10 inactive.
6 is the number of rows where a is active, not inactive.
Recount — a is active in 6 rows, so it is inactive in 16 − 6 = 10.
That overcounts; the exact number of inactive rows is 10.

generalfeedback.text: a determines p only when its term passes a through (b = true) and the other term does not mask it (c ∧ d = false): 1 × 3 × 2 = 6 active rows. The remaining 10 of 16 rows have a inactive.

name.text: Predicate with all four ICC requirements feasible

questiontext.text: For which predicate and clause are all four ICC requirements feasible?

answer.text: Clause a in p = (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d)

feedback.text: Correct — with b = false, a is inactive and p = (c ∧ d), which can be both true and false; all four requirements are reachable.

answer.text: Clause a in p = a ∧ b

feedback.text: a inactive forces p = false, so the p=true requirements are infeasible.

answer.text: Clause a in p = a ∨ b ∨ c

feedback.text: a inactive forces p = true, so the p=false requirements are infeasible.

answer.text: Clause c in p = (a ∨ b) ∧ c

feedback.text: c inactive forces p = false, so the p=true requirements are infeasible.

generalfeedback.text: All four ICC requirements are feasible only if p can be both true and false while ci is masked. In (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d) with b = false, a is masked and p = (c ∧ d) still ranges over both values, so every requirement is reachable.

name.text: RICC minor-matching scope

questiontext.text: Under RICC for p = (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d) with major clause a, the a=true and a=false requirements at p=false must share the same values of:

answer.text: All the minor clauses: b, c, and d

feedback.text: Correct — RICC pins every minor clause across the same-p pair.
RICC constrains all minor clauses, not just the one paired with a.
b is also a minor clause and must match too.
RICC's whole point is to fix the minor clauses across the pair.

generalfeedback.text: For major clause a, the minor clauses are b, c, and d. RICC requires all of them to hold identical values in the a=true and a=false tests of each same-p pair.

name.text: Feasibility condition for all four requirements

questiontext.text: The four ICC requirements for a clause ci are all feasible only if, while ci is inactive, the predicate p can be:

answer.text: Both true and false (under different inactive-making minor assignments)

feedback.text: Correct — p must range over both values while ci stays masked.
Then the p=false requirements would be infeasible.
Then the p=true requirements would be infeasible.
If ci determined p it would not be inactive; the requirements concern the masked case.

generalfeedback.text: Since ci is masked, p is set by the minor clauses. All four requirements (crossing ci with p) are feasible only when some inactive-making minor assignment yields p=true and another yields p=false.

name.text: Rows where c is inactive in (a AND b) OR c

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, clause c is inactive in exactly the assignments where:

answer.text: a = true and b = true (c either value)

feedback.text: Correct — then a ∧ b is true, masking c; p is true regardless of c.
Then a ∧ b is false, so p = c and c determines p (active).
c's own value does not decide whether c is masked; the operand a ∧ b does.
a ∧ b needs both true to mask c; either-one-true is not enough.

generalfeedback.text: c is masked in the disjunction exactly when the other operand a ∧ b is true, i.e., a = true and b = true — the 2 rows where c is inactive.

name.text: Clause with fewest inactive rows

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ c, which clause is inactive in the fewest assignments?

feedback.text: Correct — c is masked only when a ∧ b is true (2 rows), whereas a and b are each masked in 6 rows.
a is masked whenever b = false or c = true — 6 rows, more than c.
By symmetry with a, b is masked in 6 rows, more than c.

answer.text: All three are inactive equally often

feedback.text: c differs: it is masked in only 2 rows versus 6 for a and b.

generalfeedback.text: c is masked only when a ∧ b is true (2 rows). a is masked when b=false or c=true (6 rows), and b symmetrically in 6 rows. So c has the fewest inactive rows.

name.text: Total GICC requirements for a 4-clause predicate

questiontext.text: For p = (a ∧ b) ∨ (c ∧ d), where all four ICC requirements are feasible for every clause, how many inactive-clause test requirements does GICC impose in total?

feedback.text: Correct — 4 clauses × 4 requirements each = 16 test requirements.
8 = 4 clauses × 2; but ICC has four requirements per clause, not two.
4 is the requirement count for a single clause, not the whole predicate.
That doubles the count; there are 4 requirements per clause, giving 16.

generalfeedback.text: ICC imposes four requirements per major clause. With 4 clauses all feasible, GICC has 4 × 4 = 16 test requirements (some may be satisfiable by shared tests).
